tweets.text:
there's currently a bifurcation of crypto traders, those on CT & those in the trenches

memecoins are essentially a game of (3,3) the longer the associated holder group decides not to sell and the coin gets more attention from others the higher the market cap goes, this is what happened with all of the top memes last cycle, made easier by bull market and prices of other crypto assets going up across the board, but there were also a lot of memecoins that died very early last cycle and especially so before the standard was locking the LP

as this was happening and terminals got more advanced there has emerged a second group of traders who are the ones actively trading new pairs, the axiom kids who are using multiple wallets and average hold times of < 5 minutes, they realized that trading new pairs was a more consistent game to play than the (3,3) game most of CT was playing

CT needs someone to blame when coins go down, which is why pumpfun receives most of the anger from ppl on here, but it is not pumpfun who is buying these coins sub 10k mcap and selling them extremely quickly, they are just the infrastructure, & their protocol is used the most actively by this group of trenchers so a lot of their updates are for that group

whenever i mention a coin, theres a group of ppl buying afterwards who werent already in, but theres also a group of ppl selling into them that were already holding the coin, i dont frontrun my own mentions on lowcaps, i dont think thats ethical, but for the trenchers trading these things nonstop they want ppl mentioning the coins as much as possible, so they dont care if "KOL"s are multiwalleting + calling because theyre usually in the coins around the same time as them if not earlier & doing the same thing, they are aware of how pvp the game is that they're playing

the reason there are the "degen" callout rewards, as well as the "diamond" callout rewards is because pump has to provide incentives for all parts of their ecosystem, & pump cannot make the coins go up on their own, only traders agreeing to diamond hand coins to much higher market caps can, which is why that callout reward bucket is for ppl holding coins for a longer period of time and doing callouts on higher market cap tokens

being honest i didnt understand what exactly was going on in the trenches until a few months ago either because i just dont trade those coins, & i couldnt understand how pump was making so much money but it seemed like everyone on here hated them, but if you go to dv or one of the other trenchers streams you'll see they consistently have like 2k views, threadguy in comparison who is best CT streamer imo has like 20% of that because he is doing analysis on stocks, crypto, tech, but he isnt trenching new pairs, its an entirely different group of traders

solving the (3,3) game requires building something different than what pump inherently is, its what im attempting to solve with solana:9cRCn9rGT8V2imeM2BaKs13yhMEais3ruM3rPvTGpump, but i think calling someone like cupsey a rapist is dumb, he is just very good at playing the game in front of him

BREAKING: US margin debt fell -$32 billion in October amid the market's selloff, to $1.45 trillion, but remains at its 4th-highest level on record.

This follows a combined +$63 billion increase in September and August, and a -$85 billion drop in July.

Year-to-date, margin debt has surged +$223 billion, or +18%.

Since the 2022 bear market low, this metric is up +$842 billion, or +139%.

As a % of M2 money supply, margin debt now stands at 6.2%, its 3rd-highest reading since the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble of 6.4%.

Despite recent volatility, this market remains highly levered.

"History rhymes, but doesn't repeat"

There's so much rhyming going on today in comparison to the 2000 tech bubble that I'm starting to think history does repeat. This week we are about to see the second $1 trillion AI IPO hit the markets - the same event that marked the start of a Nasdaq decline in June. Credit markets are seizing up in the most vulnerable, over-levered sectors first, but there really is no panic yet though.

What I also find odd is how back then, the Y2K fears around hacks, cyberattacks and tech glitches didn't really amount to much. Whereas today, it appears AI has provided the capabilities and tooling for this fear to come to fruition and it's happening before our very eyes. FAA, NSA, Microsoft, Chase Bank, Charles Schwab, and the list goes on. All the top companies and institutions are being targeted by cyberattacks and hacks. Something is going on that the general public does not yet know about.

Buckle up.

tweets.text:
$NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply".  

- Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: 

"Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call)

This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement.  

- "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing)

(new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity)

- NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically:

Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing
B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction
Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves.

- "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track"

Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. 

- "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. 

But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

$AAOI management lost all credibility by launching another $550M ATM.

Especially after it comes contrary to earlier commentary about other financing methods + share price caution.

I still find AOI operationally compelling around their CPO program + optical transceiver ramp. 

Especially as it comes to the new China optical transceiver restrictions and incoming $5B-7B LTAs.

But I misjudged management and suffered heavy losses after cost averaging up to $100+ from the initial ~$25. 

Definitely did not foresee them tapping into abusive financing methods again after the sector drop.

I’ll still track their progress, but I don’t see how it’s possible to support a company that serially dilutes with ATMs.

I'll leave it up to your judgement. From my point of view, there's $956M in commitments vs. $605M cash so they needed more financing for their buildout. 

However two things stood out:

1. Management commentary around financing: CFO said US bank financing could reach $500m, and that profits would help fund operations. CFO said share price mattered and that they'd lean more into debt. 

So their actions went contrary to management commentary. 

If you look at $COHR, they fund capacity expansion from upfront prepayments. There's other ways to do it too like convertible notes.

2. Capital allocation issue: they spent $102M on three Texas buildings they had under lease. Which was around $5M annualized and I'm sure they're aware market financing conditions are tight. 

2 weeks after buying buildings when they were already relatively low on cash... AOI decided to do yet another $550M ATM. 

It's just a bit hard to justify.

tweets.text:
Global growth is slowing while the case for rate cuts fade.

Our global growth leading indicators dropped in October to their weakest level since early 2023. Business surveys fell sharply that month on top of ongoing drag from tighter money and credit. 

Slowdowns like this would usually push policy toward easing. However, this time inflation is getting in the way as price pressure builds again. Our US Policy LEI has fallen out of easing territory to 40.1 near the edge of a hiking regime.

That could leave the Fed facing weaker growth with little room to respond.

There is a lot of discussion today about AI recruitment. Is it all bots?

Here is how OJ is currently recruiting:

After putting out a public notice to gather proposals for an analyst, we evaluated them but then also three of us personally drove to a local Ivy League business MBA program, sat down for meetings, and talked with graduates over coffee.

That was super high signal.

After that, we followed up, and they excited our other partners in a zoom interview, or didn’t. The right people can assert themselves across multiple mediums. We’re highly engaged for super-interested talent only.

My takeaways:
-Elite employers are of course recruiting face to face. People will travel for talent, as we did.
-Elite colleges matter. Speaking for ourselves, we go to the best.
-But I was a trailer park kid. I went to state schools. I was never Ivy.
-OJ seeks out extraordinary enthusiasm and talent, but doesn’t care where it comes from if excellence is demonstrated. If someone has an extraordinary story and wants to work for us, let us know.
https://t.co/tLu7vEvP6y 

We seek to find talent in all forms, while warning that the baseline is very high.

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper
Higher yields. A strong dollar. Another difficult session for metals. But beneath the selling, the physical demand story keeps moving.

☢️ URANIUM
Bangladesh’s Rooppur 1 supplied its first electricity to the grid during commissioning today. Meanwhile, Urenco’s newly announced enrichment agreement will support Blykalla’s first U.S. reactor, with Blykalla supplying the uranium feed.

New reactors need fuel, and developers are securing supply chains years before deployment. That deserves attention beyond the daily share-price swings.

Trading around $47.3 after bouncing from Monday’s lows. Encouraging, but a modest rebound alone doesn’t establish a bottom. Watch whether silver can hold its recovery if the dollar remains strong.

🥇 GOLD
Hovering around $3,850, close to a 13-month low. Elevated Treasury yields and expectations of a December Fed hike remain major headwinds. Wednesday’s Fed minutes are the next test.

🔌 COPPER
Touched its lowest level since July as concerns over AI investment hurt sentiment. Yet China’s import premium strengthened, while immediately available copper commanded a premium on the LME. Physical supply still shows signs of tightness.

👀 NEXT UP
Nvidia beat earnings expectations after the close, reporting quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion. Watch whether that steadies sentiment in Asia, and whether tomorrow’s Fed minutes reinforce the pressure from interest rates.

My view: expensive capital can delay new mines while future demand keeps developing. I remain bullish long term, but financing strength matters enormously. A cheap mining share can become much more expensive through dilution.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

tweets.text:
Most people judge crypto payments solutions on how easy it is to spend stablecoins.

That part’s kinda solved now.

You can tap a crypto card at a restaurant and the waiter has no idea anything’s different. 

Behind that tap your money gets converted and routed so the restaurant gets paid, and you never think about it.

I wouldn’t be surprised if crypto neobanks become one of crypto’s next big product-market fits.

But what I keep thinking about is what your money’s doing the rest of the time. Like…most of it just sits there until you need to pay someone.

One project working on that is @veloprotocol, and they’re not starting from zero.

• Their Lightnet network runs that behind-the-scenes stuff across 150 countries, with 17 financial licenses and around $20B a year in volume as of 2025.

• Then there’s Orbit+, their wallet. You keep your own keys, pay with stablecoins, swap between chains in one click through SquidRouter, cash out to your bank, and there’s a card.

The part I actually find interesting is what’s NEXT. 

Velo is exploring Telegram payments, AI-agent payments, and even treasury tools that could let businesses earn yield on idle funds while keeping that money available for payments.

Imagine your business funds earning yield until you actually need to pay someone.

That's a pretty interesting direction for financial apps to take.

Of course, much of that is still on the roadmap, and actual adoption matters. 

But I think the next generation of crypto neobanks will have to offer more than just an easy way to spend stablecoins.

If someone makes that feel normal for regular people, I think it’s a much bigger deal than another card launch.

tweets.text:
🚨$NVDA cuts neocloud support plans down $1B q/q and adds tighter language around conditions; removes revenue share language from last quarter; adds new language that certain commitments "could be reduced or eliminated" if contingencies are not satisfactorily resolved. Cuts previously disclosed 2028 capex $1B to zero (sounds like a project pushout or cancellation).

Now says commitments take effect "only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us."

Previous language: "We continue to make commitments....Under these agreements we will earn revenue on upfront sale of our infra and if certain criteria are met, we will participate in revenue share."

Re: secondary equity investments, future commitments fall from $25B to $20B but 2028 plans rise from $3B --> $11B. Unclear if this is pushouts from 2027 investments not made (such as Figure AI).

Bottom line: Total commitments grew 41% QoQ, driven almost entirely by a surge in 2028 supply/capacity commitments and long-dated data center leases, but the new contingency clause means a large portion is conditional on neoclouds securing external financing.

Also 10-Q to arrive "in coming weeks" seems like a delay.

tweets.text:
$NKE case study

One of the most important lessons I’ve learned throughout my investment career, often through my own failures trying to catch falling knives, is that you should never buy a stock simply because it has fallen significantly or because it looks cheap.

Take $NKE, for example. The business has been struggling for years, and the stock has reflected that. So why buy it?

The answer cannot simply be that it’s cheap or that it’s down 50%.

You need a reason to believe something is going to change.

Maybe you’ve visited Nike stores, studied the new product lineup, or noticed improvements that the market hasn’t fully recognized yet. Whatever it is, you need a thesis for why the future will be different from the past.

This applies to every stock.

The current price already reflects the market’s collective expectations. Your edge comes from identifying something that could change those expectations.

A stock being cheap is not an investment thesis. A stock being down 50% is not a catalyst.

You don’t buy because something has gone wrong. You buy because you have a reason to believe something is about to go right.

Back in 2013 I was living in Spain, watching banks across southern Europe fail one after another. The European debt crisis was in full swing and it got bad enough that I bought a generator and filled the cupboards with tinned food.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.

tweets.text:
A user had Mutant #2129 stolen from his wallet via the PPv2 exploit.

They were not vulnerable on 9/25 because they did not have a mutant to steal. When they acquired a mutant just a few days ago, they immediately became vulnerable because they still had an open approval from years ago.

If you have open approvals to PPv2, PLEASE be sure to revoke the approvals for any collection you own, or might own in the future. PPv2 address is 0x9A1D00bEd7CD04BCDA516d721A596eb22Aac6834.

Moving forward, I have set up mempool monitoring and will be watching NFT transfers for at risk assets and executing rescues when I can. Anything rescued will be added to https://t.co/QhqhAXnJHH and claimable via the normal process.

In this particular case, the NFT was sent to BendDAO, presumably with the intention of taking out a loan. However, the attacker mistakenly sent the NFT directly to the pool contract rather than through the recognized deposit path, so it is stuck and unretrievable by the attacker or anybody else.

One path forward is for BendDAO to execute a contract upgrade to allow for the rescue of this particular NFT. I have opened a ticket in the discord and will be advocating for this path in order to return the mutant to its rightful owner.

There’s a lot of talk about agents replacing apps. I think the more interesting future is how they work together.

Word, Excel and PowerPoint are now part of the Copilot experience. And Copilot is becoming part of the apps people have loved and used for decades.

That matters because people have years of muscle memory in these tools. They know how to adjust a spreadsheet, refine a slide, edit a document. That familiarity is an enormous asset to build on.

An agent can do the research, build the model and draft the presentation. You can jump into Excel to check an assumption or PowerPoint to make the story yours, then hand the work back to the agent. Moving between delegation and doing should feel natural.

For agents to become part of everyday work, they need to meet people where they are and work with what they already know.

Apps and agents form an ecosystem. Each makes the other more useful. The agent moves the work forward, and the familiar tools let you shape the result.

Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.

The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining, chemical engineering, and more.  Me and a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017, and while it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion.  At a time when most of the seasteading community wanted to escape the US and smoke pot, this was the one project explicitly designed to make America stronger, a relief valve for ill considered or outdated rules and regulations.

I am only talking about it now because a few media outlets got wind of me and some friends topping up the coffers and plan on calling SLAB my new floating AI datacenter project. It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet.

thread_tweets.text: This data comes from 632K requests that were run from October 6 to November 8. How often do your agent sessions go cold? (4/4)
thread_tweets.full_text: This data comes from 632K requests that were run from October 6 to November 8. How often do your agent sessions go cold? (4/4)

thread_tweets.text: We found that only 1.8% of our requests were that uncached. Re-processing their context accounted for about 15% of our total Opus 5.5 spend. Most were new subagents starting from scratch, and 12% of sessions paid about $3 to resume after more than an hour idle. (3/4)
thread_tweets.full_text: We found that only 1.8% of our requests were that uncached. Re-processing their context accounted for about 15% of our total Opus 5.5 spend. Most were new subagents starting from scratch, and 12% of sessions paid about $3 to resume after more than an hour idle. (3/4)

thread_tweets.text: At 600K+ tokens, p50 time to first token was 3.5s uncached vs 1.6s cached, about 2x. However, at p90 the gap grew to 3.5x, with 10.7s uncached vs 3.1s cached. Uncached here means there were over 50K tokens the model had to process from scratch. (2/4)

Does a bigger context make your agent slower to respond?

Yes, but not by much if it's already cached. In our internal Claude usage of Opus 5.5, p50 time to first token went from 0.9s at 50–100K tokens to just 1.6s at 600K+. (1/4)🧵 https://t.co/T3D0YUO7c1

This data comes from 632K requests that were run from October 6 to November 8. How often do your agent sessions go cold? (4/4)

We found that only 1.8% of our requests were that uncached. Re-processing their context accounted for about 15% of our total Opus 5.5 spend. Most were new subagents starting from scratch, and 12% of sessions paid about $3 to resume after more than an hour idle. (3/4)

At 600K+ tokens, p50 time to first token was 3.5s uncached vs 1.6s cached, about 2x. However, at p90 the gap grew to 3.5x, with 10.7s uncached vs 3.1s cached. Uncached here means there were over 50K tokens the model had to process from scratch. (2/4)
